analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing people and small businesses into arbitration for claims under federal and state law.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 14 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on March 7, 2017 and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When you sign a credit card agreement, cell phone contract, or employment contract today, it often contains a clause saying any legal claim must be settled before a private arbitrator instead of in court. This bill would amend the Federal Arbitration Act so that a company could not force an individual or a small business into arbitration before any dispute exists if the claim involves rights created by federal or state law, the U.S. Constitution, or a state constitution. A person could still choose to arbitrate voluntarily after a dispute arises, and a judge rather than an arbitrator would decide whether an arbitration agreement is enforceable.
analysis.who_benefits: Individuals and small businesses that have legal claims against companies with which they do business or work. Today, a forced arbitration clause can mean a person cannot take a wage, discrimination, consumer, or safety claim to a judge. Under this bill, claims based on federal or state statutes or constitutional rights would go to court unless the person agreed to arbitration after the dispute arose. It would also strengthen the ability to invalidate arbitration agreements as unconscionable or otherwise unenforceable under contract law, and it would let courts void arbitration awards issued in violation of these rules [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Individuals and small businesses with legal claims

how_it_helps.text: Bars pre-dispute arbitration clauses for claims by individuals or small businesses arising from violations of federal or state statutes, the U.S. Constitution, or state constitutions [S2] [S3].
Lets a person or small business still agree to arbitration after a dispute has arisen, so voluntary arbitration remains available [S2] [S3].

Restores the ability to invalidate an arbitration agreement as unconscionable, invalid for lack of a meeting of the minds, or unenforceable under contract law or public policy, grounds that courts limited after Supreme Court decisions like AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion [S2] [S3].
Puts the decision about whether an arbitration agreement is enforceable with a court rather than an arbitrator, and lets courts vacate awards issued in violation of the new rules [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that write forced arbitration clauses into their consumer, employment, and small business contracts: banks and credit card issuers, cell phone and cable providers, nursing home chains, large employers, and other businesses. They would face more lawsuits in open court, potentially including representative claims on behalf of groups, instead of private one-on-one arbitration they currently control. Business groups have long argued that this raises litigation costs, which companies may pass on to customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, employers, and large consumer-facing companies

drawbacks.text: Companies argue that arbitration is often faster and cheaper for individuals than court litigation, and that removing forced arbitration increases litigation costs that get passed through to consumers in prices and fees. The bill's findings counter that these rulings have left millions unable to vindicate their rights, but the cost argument is a real one [S3].

The bill covers claims arising from federal or state statutes and constitutional violations by individuals and small businesses; claims based purely on ordinary contract disputes or other grievances would remain subject to pre-dispute arbitration clauses, so it is a partial fix rather than a full ban [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and concrete: it restores access to a judge for statutory and constitutional claims that forced arbitration clauses currently keep out of court, and it restores judicial review of the fairness of arbitration agreements. The main cost is more court litigation for companies, some of which may show up in prices. The bill is deliberately narrower than a total ban on forced arbitration, which limits both its benefit and its cost. For people whose biggest grievances are with employers and consumer companies on matters covered by law, the benefit outweighs the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then referred to a subcommittee, and the Congress ended without the committee ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on March 7, 2017 with 14 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1] [S3] [S4].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on March 17, 2017 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law [S1] [S5].
No further action was recorded for the rest of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies with forced arbitration clauses came out ahead. By letting the bill die in committee without a vote, they kept the status quo in which consumers, workers, and small businesses with statutory claims are routed into private arbitration under terms the company wrote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that force customers into arbitration

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar pre-dispute forced arbitration of statutory and constitutional claims by individuals and small businesses.

for.name: 14 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including senior members such as John Conyers and Maxine Waters.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up for a committee vote during the 115th Congress, leaving it with the subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor action; no version of it reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were House Democrats and there were no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-led House never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer finance companies
industries.note: These companies rely heavily on pre-dispute arbitration clauses in consumer contracts to keep disputes out of court. The bill would invalidate those clauses for statutory claims, exposing them to lawsuits from cardholders and borrowers [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Large employers with mandatory arbitration policies
industries.note: Workplace arbitration clauses covering wage, discrimination, and other statutory claims would no longer be enforceable before a dispute arises, so workers could take those claims to court [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Telecom, cable, and other consumer contract writers
industries.note: Cell phone, cable, and subscription contracts commonly force customers into arbitration; the bill would remove that barrier for claims based on law or constitution.

industries.industry: Nursing home and long-term care chains
industries.note: Admission agreements frequently require arbitration of claims involving federal and state statutes governing care; those clauses would no longer block lawsuits by residents and families.
The bill would shrink the mandatory stream of consumer and employment cases routed to private arbitrators, though voluntary post-dispute arbitration would still be allowed [S2].
